method: A case is contested on a field when at least 3 of the five candidates returned the same non-null post-gate value for that field and that value differs from the kit reference. Per-candidate values are given pre-gate (`model_value`) and post-gate (`gated_value`) with a `gate_nulled` flag. Quotes are verbatim from the cached record, clipped to 600 chars.

polarity.quote: An innkeeper is not required to entertain a guest who has refused to pay a lawful charge.
polarity.holding_summary: An innkeeper need not continue serving a guest who has refused to pay a lawful charge. Whether the disputed charge was lawful and reasonable was for the jury.

polarity.quote: An innkeeper is not required to entertain a guest who has refused to pay a lawful charge.
polarity.holding_summary: An innkeeper is not required to entertain a guest who has refused to pay a lawful charge; whether the disputed charge was excessive was for the jury. The court also held it error to admit evidence of the guest's reputation among other hotelkeepers to defeat damages.

who_was_letting.quote: An innkeeper is not required to entertain a guest who has refused to pay a lawful charge.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An innkeeper need not entertain a guest who refuses to pay a lawful charge, and whether the charge was excessive was for the jury; but the guest, if wrongfully refused service, may recover for humiliation, and evidence of his bad reputation as a hotel guest was improperly admitted.

who_was_letting.quote: An innkeeper is not required to entertain a guest who has refused to pay a lawful charge.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An innkeeper need not continue serving a guest who has refused to pay a lawful charge. Whether the disputed charge was lawful and reasonable was for the jury.

polarity.holding_summary: An innkeeper need not entertain a guest who refuses to pay a lawful charge, and whether the charge was excessive was for the jury; but the guest, if wrongfully refused service, may recover for humiliation, and evidence of his bad reputation as a hotel guest was improperly admitted.

contested.name: Byrns v. Pierce
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term

polarity.holding_summary: A tenant of a one-family cottage who vacated before midnight of the last day of the term did not hold over and was not liable for a further term's rent.
A tenant who vacated a cottage before midnight of the last day of his term was not liable as a holdover for another term.

contested.name: Barnard Realty Co. v. Bonwit
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term

polarity.holding_summary: Premises rendered untenantable by dead rats without fault of the landlord did not constitute a constructive eviction, so the tenant remained liable for rent.

polarity.quote: Where the premises are rendered untenantable without the fault of the landlord there can be no eviction.
polarity.holding_summary: Where an apartment became untenantable from the stench of dead rats without the landlord's fault, there was no constructive eviction and the tenant remained bound to pay rent.

contested.name: Conway v. Starkweather
contested.court: New York Court for the Correction of Errors

polarity.holding_summary: A tenant who holds over after a yearly demise may at the landlord's election be treated as tenant on the original terms; distraining for rent is such an election.

polarity.quote: The landlord has an election to treat him either as a trespasser, or as a tenant.
polarity.holding_summary: A tenant holding over after a yearly term may be treated by the landlord either as a trespasser or as a tenant on the original lease terms. The landlords elected to affirm the tenancy by distraining for rent after Conway remained for two weeks.

polarity.quote: Tire owner is bound to know whether his building is safe for the purposes for which he rents it, or authorizes its use, or is rotten and unsafe, and is answerable, in damages, to those who, being lawfully therein, are injured by reason of its defects, whether of original construction or caused by failure to make proper repairs.
polarity.holding_summary: An owner who rents out a lakeside "camp" is bound to know whether the building and its connecting wharf are safe for the purposes for which he rents it, and is liable in damages to persons lawfully on the premises injured by its defects. The club had rented the camp for April-June and then by the month for July and August. Judgment for the injured club member.

polarity.quote: Tire owner is bound to know whether his building is safe for the purposes for which he rents it, or authorizes its use, or is rotten and unsafe, and is answerable, in damages, to those who, being lawfully therein, are injured by reason of its defects
polarity.holding_summary: The court held the camp owner liable for injuries caused by the rotten wharf used in connection with the rented camp. The club rented the camp for several months and then continued month to month.

who_was_letting.quote: Defendant owned a double tenement cottage having four rooms and a kitchen on each side, for which, when rented to paying tenants, she received $13 and $14, per month, respectively.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court affirmed judgment for the owner because plaintiff and her husband entered and remained in a storm-damaged tenement without the owner's consent while repairs were underway. By doing so, they assumed the risks incidental to the repairs.

polarity.quote: Where one, assuming the character of tenant, without the consent of the owner, enters upon premises which are unfit for occupancy and undergoing repairs, including the repairing of plaster upon walls and ceilings saturated and loosened by stormwater, he assumes the risks incidental to such repairs, and, among them, the risk of falling plaster.
polarity.holding_summary: An occupant who moved into a storm-damaged tenement cottage against the owner's express refusal to rent it, while repairs were in progress, assumed the risk of falling plaster and could not recover. The court treated the owner's declaration that the house was 'not to be rented' as controlling on the occupant's status.

contested.name: Nash v. Springstead
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term

who_was_letting.quote: The action was commenced by the plaintiff’s testatrix in her lifetime for the rent of a house, and her executor has since been substituted as plaintiff therein.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A owner let her house to the defendant for a week or two for one dollar; the defendant declined the owner's proposal for a longer winter term but stayed on seven months. The court held it was error to exclude evidence that after the short term the defendant rented from the plaintiff's husband, a joint owner, since that evidence would rebut the presumption of acceptance of the plaintiff's longer-term proposition raised by continued occupation. The short letting of a dwelling for a week or two was treated as an ordinary, unremarkable transaction.

who_was_letting.quote: Defendant rented certain premises from plaintiff for two weeks, but declined to take them for a longer term at the price asked.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An owner's letting of a house for "a week or two" at one dollar, the occupant declining a longer monthly term, was treated as a valid short letting; continued occupancy raised only a rebuttable presumption of acceptance of the longer term. Exclusion of evidence that the occupant thereafter rented from the co-owner husband was error, so reversal was affirmed.

who_was_letting.quote: it is hereby agreed that the said parties of the first part will not rent the premises located at No. 1675 Broadway, Buffalo, N. Y., or themselves use for restaurant or rooming house purposes for a period of ten years.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A sealed covenant by adjoining owners not to rent or use their premises for restaurant or rooming house purposes for ten years was enforced by injunction, and parol evidence of an added oral consideration was inadmissible.

who_was_letting.quote: it is hereby agreed that the said parties of the first part will not rent the premises located at No. 1675 Broadway, Buffalo, N. Y., or themselves use for restaurant or rooming house purposes for a period of ten years.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court enforced a restrictive covenant barring the owners of adjoining premises from renting or using them for restaurant or rooming-house purposes for ten years. Parol evidence of an additional oral condition could not vary the sealed covenant.

who_was_letting.quote: it is hereby agreed that the said parties of the first part will not rent the premises located at No. 1675 Broadway, Buffalo, N. Y., or themselves use for restaurant or rooming house purposes for a period of ten years.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court enforced under seal a restrictive covenant by which the owners of No. 1675 Broadway agreed not to rent the premises or use them for restaurant or rooming house purposes for ten years, rejecting parol evidence of an alleged oral condition. The covenant treats rooming-house letting as a restrictable use of the property.

who_was_letting.quote: “ Now, therefore, in consideration of the premises and of the sum of one dollar, paid to the parties of the first part by the party of the second part, it is hereby agreed that the said parties of the first part will not rent the premises located at No. 1675 Broadway, Buffalo, N. Y., or themselves use for restaurant or rooming house purposes for a period of ten years.”
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A restrictive covenant under seal prohibiting the rental or use of premises for restaurant or rooming house purposes is enforceable, and parol evidence of an oral collateral agreement cannot be admitted to vary it.

contested.name: People ex rel. Waitt Operating Co. v. Goldfogle

polarity.quote: I think that the building is to be regarded as having maintained its original character of an apartment house, unaffected by the casual fact that some of the rooms are temporarily devoted to purposes which have some of the elements of hotel accommodation.
polarity.holding_summary: A fifteen-story building of one- to five-room suites, 20% of whose rooms were temporarily let to transients, remained an apartment house rather than a hotel and so qualified for the new-building tax exemption; a writ of certiorari was granted.

polarity.quote: The rooms occupied by transients, forming but twenty per cent of the total number of rooms, are being so used only temporarily in order to derive an income therefrom pending attempts to lease them for .long terms, like the rest of the rooms.
polarity.holding_summary: A building with primarily permanent tenants and only temporary transient room use remained an apartment house rather than a hotel. It therefore qualified for the new-building tax exemption available to dwellings other than hotels.

who_was_letting.quote: Where an employee occupies a room belonging to his employer as part of the consideration for his services or wages, he has no right after his discharge from his employment to continue the occupancy of the room
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An employee allowed to occupy rooms over his employer's livery stable as part of his wages had no right to remain after discharge, and the owners could put him out using no unnecessary force. But the owners were liable in trespass for wantonly stopping the chimney and forcing smoke into the rooms, injuring the occupant's wife.

who_was_letting.quote: The husband was the employee of the owner of the property. He held under him and held only during his employment, which was at the will of the owner of the property. He had no rights as a tenant under the laws regulating the landlord and tenant procedure.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that an employee's right to occupy rooms in the employer's livery building ended when his employment ended, and the employer could recover possession without liability if it used no more than ordinary force. But the employer was liable for wantonly causing smoke and gases to enter the room and injure the employee's wife.

contested.name: Cochrane v. Schryver
contested.court: New York Court of Common Pleas

polarity.quote: He had therefore no lien upon the baggage, furniture or effects of the persons to whom he let the rooms.
polarity.holding_summary: One who merely lets rooms to lodgers, without furnishing meals, is not an innkeeper and has neither the innkeeper's liability nor his lien; possession of the room and its contents remains in the lodger. Mere lodging-house keepers have no lien on lodgers' effects at common law or under New York statutes.

polarity.quote: The property upon which he claimed a lien was not in Ms possession, but in the possession of the plaintiff as the occupant of the room, and if it had been lost or stolen he would not have been responsible, as an innkeeper, for its loss.
polarity.holding_summary: One who let rooms in the upper part of a building to lodgers without supplying meals, the basement restaurant being an independent establishment leased to another, was not an innkeeper and had no lien on lodgers' effects; mere lodging-house keepers have no lien at common law or under the statutes of New York. The letting of rooms itself was treated as an ordinary, lawful activity conferring only possession on the lodger.

polarity.quote: He had therefore no lien upon the baggage, furniture or effects of the persons to whom he let the rooms.
polarity.holding_summary: A person who merely let rooms to lodgers and did not provide meals was a lodging-house keeper rather than an innkeeper. Because mere lodging-house keepers had no common-law or statutory lien on lodgers' effects, the claimed lien failed.

contested.name: Swann v. Smith
contested.court: New York Court of Common Pleas

polarity.quote: the justice was right if he held that the plaintiff was lacking in ordinary care in leaving his door unlocked when he knew that the hall-door was also open to all who chose to enter
polarity.holding_summary: The keeper of a bathing-house whose upper floors were let in apartments to lodgers was not liable for clothing stolen from a lodger's room; a lodging-house keeper does not take the lodger's goods into his custody, and in any event the lodger's own failure to lock his door barred recovery.

polarity.quote: There is authority for holding that a lodging-house keeper, like the defendant, does not assume responsibility for the goods of his lodger, as he does not take them into his custody
polarity.holding_summary: The keeper of a bathing-house whose upper floors were let in apartments to lodgers was not liable for property stolen from a lodger's room by persons unknown, where the lodger left his own door unlocked knowing the hall-door was open. A lodging-house keeper does not assume responsibility for the goods of his lodger, as he does not take them into his custody.

polarity.quote: There is authority for holding that a lodging-house keeper, like the defendant, does not assume responsibility for the goods of his lodger, as he does not take them into his custody
polarity.holding_summary: The bathing-house keeper who let upper-floor apartments to lodgers was not liable for theft from the plaintiff's room. The plaintiff's own failure to keep the room locked constituted a lack of ordinary care.

contested.name: Devonshire Associates v. Garrett
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term

who_was_letting.quote: the prior owner permitted the occupancy of the apartments by roomers and thus expressly waived the covenant of the leases that the premises be occupied “ osa strictly private family dwelling apartment by said tenant, and the tenant’s immediate family only-”.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court reversed eviction orders based on roomers' single-room occupancy. The prior owner had waived the private-family occupancy covenant, and the cited housing department letter stated that four roomers did not violate the Multiple Dwelling Law.

who_was_letting.quote: the evidence establishes that the prior owner permitted the occupancy of the apartments by roomers and thus expressly waived the covenant of the leases that the premises be occupied “ osa strictly private family dwelling apartment by said tenant, and the tenant’s immediate family only-”.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The Appellate Term reversed holdover and single-room-occupancy eviction orders against tenants whose apartments were occupied by roomers, because the prior owner had permitted roomer occupancy and waived the 'strictly private family dwelling apartment' covenant, and the housing department stated the occupancy was not in violation. The petitions were dismissed.

who_was_letting.quote: the evidence establishes that the prior owner permitted the occupancy of the apartments by roomers and thus expressly waived the covenant of the leases
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Eviction petitions charging tenants with unlawful single-room occupancy were dismissed: the prior owner had permitted occupancy by roomers and thereby waived the private-family covenant, and the housing department itself stated the apartment occupied by four roomers was not in violation of the Multiple Dwelling Law. Notice requirements were also unmet.

who_was_letting.quote: Further, as to the charge of single-room occupancy in violation of sections 82 and 248 of the Multiple Dwelling Law the evidence establishes that the prior owner permitted the occupancy of the apartments by roomers and thus expressly waived the covenant of the leases that the premises be occupied “ osa strictly private family dwelling apartment by said tenant, and the tenant’s immediate family only-”.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Eviction proceedings against tenants for keeping roomers in alleged violation of single-room occupancy restrictions under the Multiple Dwelling Law were dismissed where the prior owner had waived the single-family lease restriction. Letting rooms to four roomers was not an illegal purpose justifying eviction.

who_was_letting.quote: On April 1,1886, defendant procured from plaintiff, as agent of his wife, a written lease for the premises for three years.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court affirmed a judgment for the landlord in an action for rent under a written three-year lease. Whether the landlord's agent had authority to accept the tenant's asserted surrender was properly submitted to the jury.

contested.name: City of New York v. New York & Hong Kong Reciprocation Exchange Corp.

polarity.quote: the court finds that these 55 persons cannot be deemed “tenants” of this basement room which contained only approximately 20 beds.
polarity.holding_summary: Fifty-five persons relocated by the City from illegal cubicles in the basement of a commercial building were not 'tenants' under the Administrative Code relocation provisions, so the owner was not liable for the City's $284,861.95 in relocation expenses and the lien was cancelled. The court reasoned that 'tenant' connotes greater rights than 'occupant' or licensee and that the basement was in no sense a permanent residence. The decision narrows occupant protections against an owner.

polarity.quote: Although the relocation services provided by the City to the aforesaid 55 persons clearly reflect humanitarian efforts by our City government to aid people who had no true residence, the court finds that these 55 persons cannot be deemed “tenants” of this basement room which contained only approximately 20 beds.
polarity.holding_summary: Occupants of unhabitable basement cubicles vacated pursuant to a fire department vacate order were not statutory tenants under the Administrative Code relocation reimbursement provisions. The property owner was therefore not liable to reimburse the City for tenant relocation costs.

contested.name: People v. Reilly
contested.court: New York Court of Special Sessions

who_was_letting.quote: Any disputed words in a tax statute must be construed against the taxing power.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A motel is not a hotel, apartment hotel or lodging house within the city occupancy tax provisions, which must be strictly construed against the taxing power. The information charging failure to register and file returns was dismissed and the defendant discharged.

who_was_letting.quote: a motel, as one generally understands the term, and as typified by the building sought to be erected by this petition, merely furnishes the transient guest with sleeping quarters and bath and toilet facilities, with linen service and a place to park his car.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court dismissed tax charges against a motel operator, holding that a motel was distinct from a hotel and lodging house under the city tax law. The court concluded that the municipality had to include motels specifically if it sought to tax them.

contested.name: Broome County Co-Operative Fire Insurance v. Kendall
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

polarity.quote: The record amply supports Supreme Court’s conclusion that the family home care provided was not engaged in for profit and, therefore, did not constitute a business pursuit.
polarity.holding_summary: Householders who provided room, board and family care for developmentally disabled persons in their own home were not engaged in a "business pursuit" and the disabled persons were not "roomers or boarders," so the home did not become business property under the homeowner's policy exclusions. The insurer must defend and indemnify.

polarity.quote: The record amply supports Supreme Court’s conclusion that the family home care provided was not engaged in for profit and, therefore, did not constitute a business pursuit.
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that family home care for developmentally disabled persons was not shown to be a profit-making business pursuit. It also held that the residents were not roomers or boarders, so the home was not converted into business property under the insurance policy.

who_was_letting.quote: The Vortkamps provided home health care for developmentally disabled persons at their home in Broome County as family home care providers for the Broome District Developmental Services of the State Office of Mental Retardation and Developmental Disabilities.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Householders who provided room, board and family care for developmentally disabled persons in their own home were not engaged in a "business pursuit" and the disabled persons were not "roomers or boarders," so the home did not become business property under the homeowner's policy exclusions. The insurer must defend and indemnify.

who_was_letting.quote: The evidence indicates that the disabled persons were treated and accepted as family members and supports Supreme Court’s conclusion that they were not roomers or boarders under the policy.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that family home care for developmentally disabled persons was not shown to be a profit-making business pursuit. It also held that the residents were not roomers or boarders, so the home was not converted into business property under the insurance policy.

contested.name: Shienker v. Cox
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term

polarity.quote: The landlord respondent having rented part of the dwelling unit for housekeeping purposes, the housing accommodation was occupied for other than single-family occupancy and the exemption from control terminated.
polarity.holding_summary: Because the landlord let part of his own dwelling unit for housekeeping purposes, the unit was occupied for other than single-family occupancy and the exemption from rent control terminated. The eviction petition was dismissed and a final order awarded the tenant.

polarity.quote: The landlord respondent having rented part of the dwelling unit for housekeeping purposes, the housing accommodation was occupied for other than single-family occupancy and the exemption from control terminated.
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that the landlord's housekeeping letting in part of a one- or two-family dwelling ended the decontrol exemption. It reversed the landlord's order and dismissed the petition in favor of the tenant.

who_was_letting.quote: The premises here, formerly occupied as a rooming house, were altered and converted into a five-family Class A multiple dwelling
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that the administrator could not apply a conversion restriction aimed at rooming-house accommodations converted after April 30, 1962 to a conversion completed before that date. It remanded for de novo administrative consideration, while recognizing the administrator's authority over dangerous or substandard accommodations.

who_was_letting.quote: no order shall be issued by the Administrator decontrolling housing accommodations (1) of any type resulting from conversion after April 30, 1962 of rooming house accommodations or of single room occupancy accommodations
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Landlords who converted a former rooming house into a five-family Class A multiple dwelling before the April 30, 1962 regulatory cut-off sought decontrol, which the City Rent Administrator denied. The court doubted that the amended regulation barring decontrol of rooming-house conversions applied retroactively to a completed pre-amendment conversion and remanded for de novo consideration.

polarity.quote: The application is denied, and the proceeding is dismissed.
polarity.holding_summary: Although converted rooming houses are not categorically barred from decontrol, this owner failed to show the conversion was completed before April 30, 1962, that the new units met the 395 square foot minimum, or that additional housing accommodations were created. The Administrator's denial of decontrol was sustained and the article 78 proceeding dismissed.

polarity.quote: Sufficient ground exists upon the record herein to support the order and it should not be disturbed.
polarity.holding_summary: The court upheld denial of decontrol after conversion of a rooming house into apartments. The owner failed to establish timely conversion, adequate unit size, or an increase in the number of legal housing accommodations.

polarity.quote: the landlord is bound to know whether his building is safe for the purposes for which he rents or authorizes its use, and is answerable .to those who, being lawfully therein, are injured by reason of its defects, whether of original construction or failure to make proper repairs
polarity.holding_summary: A lumber company that rented a dwelling to plaintiffs was answerable for the death of their infant child caused by a nail protruding from a wall, because under the Louisiana Civil Code the lessor must know whether his building is safe and must keep it safe for occupancy. Exception of no cause of action overruled.

polarity.quote: the landlord is bound to know whether his building is safe for the purposes for which he rents or authorizes its use, and is answerable .to those who, being lawfully therein, are injured by reason of its defects
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that the parents' allegations stated a cause of action against the corporate lessor for their child's death from a protruding nail in a rented dwelling. Under Louisiana law, a lessor must deliver and maintain leased premises in safe condition for their intended occupancy.

polarity.quote: The daughter, Josephine, before and after her marriage, worked as a laundress and had boarders and lodgers, for whom she did the cooking.
polarity.holding_summary: In a succession dispute the court found the mother's sale of her home to her daughter was a disguised donation subject to collation, and that a son long recognized as a brother was presumed legitimate. The daughter's taking of boarders and lodgers in the family dwelling, and the earnings from that boarding house, were recounted without question as a legitimate source of family income.

who_was_letting.quote: One of the boarders slept in the shack where Richard Kelly lived, and five of them slept in the house occupied by the mother and daughter.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: In a succession dispute the court found the mother's sale of her home to her daughter was a disguised donation subject to collation, and that a son long recognized as a brother was presumed legitimate. The daughter's taking of boarders and lodgers in the family dwelling, and the earnings from that boarding house, were recounted without question as a legitimate source of family income.

contested.name: Orville Realty Co. v. Warnick
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term

who_was_letting.quote: The premises leased included a house occupied by defendant and his family, another house occupied by his chauffeur, and a garage.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Where the parties to a lease of premises from May to November as a summer home were indifferent to winter occupancy, the law would not imply a renewal tenancy from the tenant's leaving furniture on the premises, and the owner's claim for winter use and occupation was dismissed. A seasonal letting was treated as complete on its own terms, generating no implied continuation.

who_was_letting.quote: it was perfectly clear to both plaintiff and defendant that the lease was intended to be merely that of a summer home
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A seasonal May-to-November lease of a summer home did not give rise to an implied renewal or liability for use and occupation over the winter, since both parties contemplated only summer occupancy and the owner took possession through a caretaker.

who_was_letting.quote: Obviously no extensive discussion is required to point out the distinction between the ordinary dwelling house where persons make their permanent homes and hotels and rooming houses, mainly occupied by transient guests.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The 1920 Housing Laws suspending ejectment and holdover proceedings and permitting the defense of unjust rent were sustained as a valid exercise of the police power in an emergency; a monthly tenant of an apartment could remain on paying reasonable rent, and the owner's motion for judgment was denied.

who_was_letting.quote: The averments of the complainant, a domestic corporation, briefly stated, are that as owner of premises No. 435 East Sixty-sixth street, a dwelling house
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The Housing Laws of 1920 (chs. 942, 944, 945, 947) were held constitutional: the police power permits suspension of the owner's remedy of ejectment and regulation of rents during the housing emergency, so the owner's motion for judgment on the pleadings in ejectment against a monthly tenant was denied. The court reasoned that absolute ownership carries a reciprocal duty to manage use for the common good.

contested.name: Carhart v. Ryder
contested.court: New York Court of Common Pleas

who_was_letting.quote: who stated that she wanted the premises for the purpose of renting the same for furnished lodgings
who_was_letting.holding_summary: In an action by a landlord against a surety for rent of a furnished house, alleged fraud in failing to disclose the premises' bad reputation as a former house of prostitution was no defense where the tenant entered and remained in possession without repudiating the contract of letting. The landlord's rent claim on the furnished-house letting, taken for the purpose of letting furnished lodgings, was enforced.

who_was_letting.quote: in an action by a landlord against a surety for the rent of a furnished house, alleged fraud on the part of the landlord, in neglecting to disclose to the tenant the bad reputation of the premises as a house of prostitution, does not constitute a defense, where the tenant has entered and remained in possession without repudiating the contract of letting
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A tenant who hired a furnished house in order to let furnished lodgings, and who remained in possession without repudiating the letting, cannot resist rent on the ground that the landlord concealed the house's bad reputation. Judgment for the landlord against the surety was affirmed.

polarity.quote: the maintenance of a private hotel or boarding-house, in which the furnishing of food and liquor to its guests, to be served with their meals or in their private rooms, was only incidental to the principal business there carried on, was not a violation of the covenants in question.
polarity.holding_summary: Operating a private hotel or boarding house for permanent guests did not violate a covenant against business uses where food and liquor service was incidental. The court enjoined the separate annex operation because it was a public restaurant and drinking saloon rather than guest lodging.

polarity.quote: the court held that the maintenance of a private hotel or boarding-house, in which the furnishing of food and liquor to its guests, to be served with their meals or in their private rooms, was only incidental to the principal business there carried on, was not a violation of the covenants in question.
polarity.holding_summary: Under restrictive covenants barring business use, the court enjoined operation of a standalone restaurant and drinking saloon but affirmed (following Murray v. Charman) that keeping a private hotel or boarding-house, with food and liquor furnished only incidentally to guests, is not a violation. Boarding-house keeping was treated as compatible with the residential character of the restricted tract.

polarity.quote: the maintenance of a private hotel or boarding-house, in which the furnishing of food and liquor to its guests, to be served with their meals or in their private rooms, was only incidental to the principal business there carried on, was not a violation of the covenants in question
polarity.holding_summary: Under a covenant barring business uses, keeping a private hotel or boarding house where food and liquor were served to guests incidentally was not a violation, but operating the annex as a public restaurant and drinking saloon was, and was enjoined; plaintiff had not lost the benefit of the covenant.

polarity.quote: the maintenance of a private hotel or boarding-house, in which the furnishing of food and liquor to its guests, to be served with their meals or in their private rooms, was only incidental to the principal business there carried on, was not a violation of the covenants in question.
polarity.holding_summary: Court enforced a restrictive covenant prohibiting use of land as a restaurant/saloon, but held that operating a private hotel/boarding house for permanent guests where food and liquor were incidental to lodging did not violate the covenant. The case affirms that letting rooms and board to long-term paying guests as a private hotel/boarding house is a lawful use not barred by a covenant restricting commercial/business use.

polarity.quote: The Kolping Society evicted Stiles without a summary proceeding and without a court order.
polarity.holding_summary: A former employee who remained in a rooming house room and paid rent for six months after discharge was a tenant under RPAPL 711 and could be removed only by summary proceeding. The rooming house operator's self-help lockout was unlawful and damages, including for emotional distress, were awarded.

polarity.quote: The Kolping Society evicted Stiles without a summary proceeding and without a court order.
polarity.holding_summary: A former employee who remained in a rooming house and paid rent became a tenant at will. The operator's self-help lockout violated RPAPL 711, and the court awarded damages.

polarity.quote: The Kolping Society evicted Stiles without a summary proceeding and without a court order. Thus, the defendant was in direct violation of the procedure set forth in the statute.
polarity.holding_summary: A former employee who remained as a rent-paying tenant in a rooming house room for over 30 days was held to be a statutory tenant under RPAPL 711, entitled to a summary proceeding before eviction; the rooming house's self-help eviction (changing locks, removing belongings) was unlawful and supported an award of damages.

contested.name: Smith v. Rector of St. Philip's Church

who_was_letting.quote: the plaintiff occupied one range of rooms and let the other appartments to tenants by the month.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A lessee who built an apartment house, occupied one range of rooms himself, and let the other apartments to tenants by the month did not forfeit the lease by under-letting; the lessor's years of accepting rent with knowledge of the use was construed as a license to use the building as an apartment house. The court held that letting rooms to lodgers is not a breach of a covenant against under-letting, and that an apartment occupier has merely the right to occupy designated rooms for the time specified.

who_was_letting.quote: It was shown on the trial that the house erected by the plaintiff was an apartment house, and that the plaintiff occupied one range of rooms and let the other apartments to tenants by the month, by verbal lease, the rent being exacted each month in advance.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A lessee who himself occupied one range of rooms and let the other apartments of his apartment house to monthly tenants did not breach the covenant against under-letting; letting rooms to lodgers is not an under-letting, and the lessor's long receipt of rent with knowledge operated as a license. The lessee was therefore entitled to enforce the renewal/appraisal option.

who_was_letting.quote: the plaintiff occupied one range of rooms and let the other appartments to tenants by the month, by verbal lease, the rent being exacted each month in advance
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The lessee built an apartment house and let apartments to tenants by the month; the court held this monthly letting of rooms to lodgers did not violate a lease covenant against subletting or underletting, characterizing the interest of a room-occupant as peculiar and akin to lodging rather than a lease/assignment triggering forfeiture.

contested.name: Douglass v. Seiferd
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term

polarity.quote: it seems clear to us that the hiring was by the year, that there was no valid surrender, and that the landlord was entitled to a verdict
polarity.holding_summary: A flat hired "at the rate of" $35 a month with rent paid a year and then six months in advance was a yearly, not monthly, tenancy, and leaving keys with an unauthorized janitress was no surrender. The landlord was entitled to a verdict and the order setting aside the jury's contrary verdict was affirmed.

contested.name: Humphreys v. Gardner
contested.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature

polarity.quote: The parties claiming respectively the right to let, interpleaded, as it were, in his presence, and agreed to refer the question to the arbitrators
polarity.holding_summary: Where two claimants each asserted the right to let the house and submitted that question to arbitrators in the tenant's presence, the tenant who entered with knowledge of the submission was bound to notice the award directing rent to be paid to the successful claimant.

polarity.quote: the parties claiming respectively the right to let, interpleaded, as it were, in his presence, and agreed to refer the question to the arbitrators
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that Humphreys was bound by the arbitration determining which competing claimant had the right to let the house and receive the ensuing year's rent. Because he entered possession knowing of and approving the submission, notice of the award was unnecessary.

contested.name: Abeel & Abeel v. Radcliff
contested.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature

polarity.holding_summary: Measure of recovery for use and occupation where a tenant holds over after a ground lease and the landlord has become entitled to the buildings.

polarity.quote: where a tenant holds over, without any new stipulation between the parties, an implication arises that there is a tacit consent on both sides, that the tenant shall hold, from year to year, at the former or first rent.
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that a holdover tenant ordinarily implies consent to a year-to-year tenancy at the former rent. On the particular facts, however, the owners could recover the actual value of the house and lot because the original rent had covered only the lot and the owners had since acquired title to the buildings.

contested.name: Jones v. Clark
contested.court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature

polarity.holding_summary: A tenant of a mortgagor may attorn to and take a lease from the mortgagee after forfeiture and plead that attornment against the mortgagor's claim for rent.
A lessor may distrain under a parol demise; a parol lease for seven years void by the statute of frauds enures as a tenancy from year to year on the stated terms.

polarity.quote: A lessor may distrain upon a parol demise, he having the reversion, without any special agreement empowering him to distrain.
polarity.holding_summary: A landlord with the reversion could distrain for rent under a parol demise. Although a seven-year oral demise was void as a lease for that term, entry and holding under it created a year-to-year tenancy governed by its rental terms.

who_was_letting.quote: The plaintiff was an innkeeper in the village of Orville.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An innkeeper is bound to receive and entertain travellers and is answerable as insurer for a guest's goods; in exchange the law gives him a lien on the guest's goods for his reasonable charges. But the lien (and liability) exist only where the owner of the goods is actually or constructively a guest; an innkeeper who merely boards a neighbor's horses at livery, the neighbor retaining use at pleasure, has no lien. Judgment against the innkeeper affirmed.

who_was_letting.quote: An innkeeper is bound to receive and entertain travellers, and is answerable for the goods of a guest although they may be stolen or lost without any fault on his part; and, on account of this extraordinary liability, the law gives him a lien on the goods for the satisfaction of his reasonable charges.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An innkeeper must receive and entertain travellers and, because of his insurer's liability for a guest's goods, has a lien on them; but neither liability nor lien exists unless the owner of the goods is actually or constructively a guest. Since the horses belonged to a neighbor who was never a guest, the plaintiff stood as a mere livery keeper and had no lien.
Concerns an innkeeper's lien over horses and the definition of 'guest' status for purposes of innkeeper liability; does not address letting of dwellings/rooms to lodgers for pay.

polarity.quote: when the owner of a parcel of land in a town or city occupied by him as the homestead of his family permanently devotes a part thereof to a purpose inconsistent with its use as a part of his homestead, and permanently abandons such use, the parcel so set apart ceases to be a part of the homestead
polarity.holding_summary: Where a town homestead owner rented out an adjoining house on the same block, the middle lot retained its homestead character because he continued using its cistern for family purposes, but the east lot, built expressly for rental income and never used domestically, was permanently devoted to a non-homestead use and lost its exemption. Renting for income was thus treated as a use inconsistent with home use as to the abandoned parcel.

polarity.quote: when the owner of a parcel of land in a town or city occupied by him as the homestead of his family permanently devotes a part thereof to a purpose inconsistent with its use as a part of his homestead, and permanently abandons such use, the parcel so set apart ceases to be a part of the homestead.
polarity.holding_summary: An owner residing on part of a town block rented out two other houses on the block, one as a boarding house and one built expressly to rent for income. The court held the middle lot (old house, including boarding-house rental with continued domestic use of its cistern) remained part of the homestead, but the east lot, permanently devoted to renting for revenue, was abandoned as homestead and subject to forced sale. Letting for income was treated as a use inconsistent with homestead protection.

polarity.quote: For some time he rented the old house as a boarding house, and he and his family took their meals with the tenants.
polarity.holding_summary: A homestead owner rented out one house as a boarding house (living and taking meals with the boarders) and another as a permanent rental, and the court treated such renting as an ordinary and lawful use of the property, though permanent devotion of a lot to rental purposes could remove it from homestead protection. The owner's freedom to rent was assumed lawful; the dispute concerned only homestead exemption from execution.

polarity.quote: If it had appeared that appellee was occupying the house as a mere: tenant at will the charge would have been incorrect, in that under it the jury would have understood that if such was the relation of the parties-it was the right of appellant to lock the house with the property of - appellee in it and to be bound to no diligence whatever for its preservation. Such a charge was properly refused.
polarity.holding_summary: The occupant of the upper story of the owner's building was not a tenant at will but a joint occupant under a partnership agreement, and the owner had no right to change the locks and shut him out; even a tenancy at will would have required some care by the landlord for the occupant's property on terminating the estate. Actual and exemplary damages against the owner were affirmed.

polarity.quote: Appellee is shown to have been entitled to the occupancy of the house at the time its doors were closed upon him.
polarity.holding_summary: The court affirmed damages against the building owner for locking his business partner and the partner's family out of upper-story residential rooms. It held that the evidence showed joint occupancy rather than a tenancy at will and that the owner could not exclude the occupant and retain his property without right.

who_was_letting.quote: Appellant and appellee were together engaged in a retail drug business in a house belonging to appellant, the lower story of which was occupied as a drug store and the upper story by appellee and his wife as a residence
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A drug-store partner resided with his wife in the upper story of a building owned by the other partner, who occupied the lower story; the owner changed the locks and shut the occupant out. The court affirmed actual and exemplary damages, holding the arrangement was a joint occupancy under a partnership agreement, not a tenancy at will, and that even a tenancy at will would have required the owner to use care toward the occupant's property on termination. The owner's self-help exclusion was condemned.

who_was_letting.quote: The evidence, however, did not tend to show that appellee was a tenant at will or even strictly a tenant at all, but did tend to show a joint-occupancy of the house for the conduct of a business in which they were-both interested
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The occupant of the upper story of the owner's building was not a tenant at will but a joint occupant under a partnership agreement, and the owner had no right to change the locks and shut him out; even a tenancy at will would have required some care by the landlord for the occupant's property on terminating the estate. Actual and exemplary damages against the owner were affirmed.

who_was_letting.quote: The evidence, however, did not tend to show that appellee was a tenant at will or even strictly a tenant at all, but did tend to show a joint-occupancy of the house for the conduct of a business in which they were-both interested, which made it necessary as well as proper for the conduct of the business that appellee should remain there until the business-ceased, and his possession for this purpose of the upper story was to some- . extent exclusive, but in the act of excluding him from that part jointly occupied appellant excluded him from the entire house.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court affirmed damages against the building owner for locking his business partner and the partner's family out of upper-story residential rooms. It held that the evidence showed joint occupancy rather than a tenancy at will and that the owner could not exclude the occupant and retain his property without right.

contested.name: Stewart v. McCready
contested.court: New York Court of Common Pleas

who_was_letting.quote: The intent of the statute of 1860, (Sess, Laws, 771,) giving to the keeper of a boarding house a lien to the extent of the board due, is, to give them the same lien which an inn-keeper has upon the effects of a guest, without reference to the character of the guests, whether they are transient ox permanent boarders.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The 1860 act gives boarding-house keepers the innkeeper's lien on their boarders' effects without regard to whether the occupant is a transient guest or a boarder by the week or month. Judgment denying the keeper's lien was reversed.

who_was_letting.quote: A boarding-house keeper, as contradistinguished from the keeper of an inn, should, in the sense of this statute, be regarded as one who furnishes accommodation for a definite period, as by the week or month, at a rate of compensation agreed upon.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The 1860 statute gave boarding-house keepers an innkeeper-like lien for unpaid board without distinguishing between transient and permanent boarders. A boarding-house keeper was defined as one furnishing accommodation for a definite period, such as by the week or month, at an agreed rate.

contested.name: Prendorill v. Kennedy
contested.court: New York Court of Common Pleas

who_was_letting.quote: The plaintiff in this case keeps a public house on Hubert street, for the entertainment and lodging of travelers.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court refused to enjoin the superintendent of police and a precinct captain from stationing officers in front of a public house that lodged travelers and warning strangers 'to be careful' after repeated complaints of exorbitant and illegal charges. The police supervision was held a valid exercise of the duty to protect strangers and emigrants. The keeper's request to shield his lodging business from police oversight was rejected.

who_was_letting.quote: The plaintiff in this case keeps a public house on Hubert street, for the entertainment and lodging of travelers.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court refused to enjoin the metropolitan police from stationing officers outside plaintiff's public house and warning prospective guests to 'be careful,' finding this a lawful exercise of the police's statutory duty to protect strangers, notwithstanding the innkeeper's complaint that it injured his business.

contested.name: Toub v. Schmidt
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term

polarity.quote: He was not at. the defendant’s house for refreshment or rest, or with an intention to remain.
polarity.holding_summary: A peddler who merely left a pack at an inn, without taking a room, food, or drink, did not become an inn guest. The court reversed a judgment against the innkeeper because the innkeeper-and-guest relationship had not been established.

polarity.quote: and although it is not easy to determine, either from principle or authority, precisely what conduct will be sufficient to make a guest, yet it seems plain that one who is not to be entertained, and who has not adopted the inn as a temporary home, is not a guest, within the meaning of the law, so as to entitle him to the severe remedies enforced against innkeepers.
polarity.holding_summary: A pack peddler who left goods at an inn but engaged no room and neither ate nor drank there was not a guest, so the innkeeper's extraordinary liability did not attach.

who_was_letting.quote: Von Behren held out and offered for rent the said camp, with said connecting wharf, as a place of resort and recreation
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that the petition stated a cause of action against the owner of a resort camp for injury to a guest caused by collapse of the connecting wharf. The owner had offered the camp for rent and remained responsible for unsafe conditions affecting persons lawfully present.

contested.name: Blair v. Blair
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

polarity.quote: But the husband who maintains the family has a right to say who shall reside with them in the home, and may refuse to have boarders whose requirements interfere with the family comfort and whose presence excites comment on the part of the neighbors.
polarity.holding_summary: Taking a boarder and letting a furnished room in the family home was treated as a household matter within the husband's right to regulate, even though the house was jointly owned; the wife's departure was not justified and the separation decree was reversed.

polarity.quote: the husband who maintains the family has a right to say who shall reside with them in the home, and may refuse to have boarders whose requirements interfere with the family comfort
polarity.holding_summary: In a separation action, the court held that a husband who maintains the family has the right to decide what persons outside the family shall share the home, including refusing boarders, even in a jointly owned house. Taking a boarder and letting a furnished room were treated as ordinary household incidents, and the wife's conduct did not justify separation.

polarity.quote: Defendant, therefore, wished to give up taking boarders and have the privacy that they had before enjoyed.
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that the husband who maintained the family could decide that boarders would not share the jointly owned home. The wife's taking of a boarder and letting of a furnished room thus could be stopped as part of the husband's authority to regulate the household.

contested.name: State v. City Sav. Bank & Trust Co.

who_was_letting.quote: In our view, the Legislature has not levied a license tax against one who leases his own property, or against a banking concern,' which is the case here, that leases its surplus space for offices in the building owned by it.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The omnibus clause of the 1924 and 1926 license acts does not impose a license tax on an owner (here a bank) that leases surplus space in its own building for offices. The court added that a license tax on leasing one's own property would doubtfully be constitutional, since the right to lease one's property is an incident of ownership and such a tax would be a property tax in disguise.

who_was_letting.quote: The lower part of the building is used by it for its banking business proper, and the upper part, which its present needs do not require, is leased to various persons for offices.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that the omnibus license-tax provisions did not tax a bank's leasing of surplus office space in its own building. It stated that the Legislature did not intend to impose such a license and observed that the right to lease one's own property may be an incident of ownership.

contested.name: Keesey v. O'Reilly
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

polarity.quote: the circumstances constituted the deceased a mere licensee
polarity.holding_summary: A weekly subtenant of two furnished rooms had no easement over the roof, and her use of it to dry clothes made her a mere licensee, so the owner was not liable for her death when a chimney fell; judgment against the owner was reversed and the complaint dismissed.

polarity.quote: the only legal inference properly to be drawn from these facts, in the light of all of the other facts in the case above referred to, is that the defendant acquiesced in and permitted such use of the roof, thus imposing upon the defendant a duty to exercise only such care as is owing to a bare licensee.
polarity.holding_summary: A weekly subtenant of two furnished rooms had no easement to use the roof for drying clothes. At most, the owner had merely permitted roof use, so the deceased was a licensee and the negligence judgment against the owner was dismissed.

polarity.quote: But the tax in contest is not invalid, for any of the reasons assigned in the appellant’s argument that it is a direct tax upon the property, because in fact it is not a direct tax upon the property, but a license tax upon the business in which the property is used or employed.
polarity.holding_summary: The court upheld a license tax on the business of operating an office building, holding that such operation is a recognized occupation or business rather than a tax on property merely because of ownership. It reduced the tax calculation to revenues from office-building operations, excluding rent from retail-store portions of the property.

polarity.quote: It is plain, therefore, that the doubt which the court expressed, in State v. City Savings Bank & Trust Co., as to whether a license tax on the business of operating an office building would be really a direct tax upon the property itself, was not essential to the question before the court, and was not a part of the decision rendered in the case.
polarity.holding_summary: The court upheld a statutory license tax of one-tenth of one percent on gross rents from operating an office building, rejecting the owner's argument that renting property is an inherent attribute of ownership. It limited the tax to revenues from the office-building business proper, excluding ground-floor retail rents, and expressly confined the incident-of-ownership dictum in State v. City Savings Bank as non-essential.

who_was_letting.quote: But the tax in contest is not invalid, for any of the reasons assigned in the appellant’s argument that it is a direct tax upon the property, because in fact it is not a direct tax upon the property, but a license tax upon the business in which the property is used or employed.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A license tax on the business of operating an office building and deriving revenue therefrom is a valid excise tax, not a direct property tax or income tax. The court limited the earlier City Savings Bank dictum that leasing one's own property is an incident of ownership, calling it unnecessary to that decision, while conceding that an isolated leasing by an owner would not be a taxable business. The tax was, however, computed only on revenue from the office-building business.

who_was_letting.quote: But the operating or managing of an office building, whether by the owner or by a lessee of the building, is now well recognized as the carrying on of an occupation or business.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court upheld a license tax on the business of operating an office building, holding that such operation is a recognized occupation or business rather than a tax on property merely because of ownership. It reduced the tax calculation to revenues from office-building operations, excluding rent from retail-store portions of the property.

polarity.quote: In other words, from defendant’s judicial admission it is clear that the transaction, although disguised as a sale in which he was named as a copurchaser, was in truth and in fact an onerous donation.
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that the transfer of a one-half interest in the house was an onerous donation conditioned on the donees' providing Garcia room, board, laundry, and care. It set aside the transfer because the donees failed to perform those conditions.

who_was_letting.quote: he moved into the home of 'defendant on Community Street in New 'Orleans under an arrangement by which he paid Mr. and Mrs. Dulcich $35 a month for room and board
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An elderly dentist's conveyance of a half interest in a house to a couple, in exchange for their promise to furnish him room, board, laundry, and care for life, was an onerous donation that could be revoked when they ceased to provide those services. The court treated room-and-board arrangements—both the earlier $35-a-month boarding and the plaintiff's later status as a paying guest elsewhere—as ordinary, lawful household arrangements.

who_was_letting.quote: He had been living in St. Bernard Parish, but on April 6, 1956, he moved into the home of 'defendant on Community Street in New 'Orleans under an arrangement by which he paid Mr. and Mrs. Dulcich $35 a month for room and board.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that the transfer of a one-half interest in the house was an onerous donation conditioned on the donees' providing Garcia room, board, laundry, and care. It set aside the transfer because the donees failed to perform those conditions.

contested.name: Smiley v. Williams
contested.court: Civil Court of the City of New York

who_was_letting.quote: Petitioner acknowledges that respondent has been living in the subject premises since October 2008.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The owner consented to the respondent's continued occupancy and therefore could not remove him as a squatter. Continuous residence for more than six months made the respondent a permanent rent-stabilized tenant entitled to a lease.

who_was_letting.quote: Section 2520.6 (j) of the Rent Stabilization Code (9 NYCRR) defines a permanent tenant as an individual who has “continuously resided in the same building as a principal residence for a period of at least six months.”
who_was_letting.holding_summary: In a squatter holdover proceeding concerning an SRO building, the court held that an occupant who continuously resided in the building for six months became a 'permanent tenant' under Rent Stabilization Code § 2520.6(j), even though the owner denied receiving rent or making any agreement. The owner's claimed owner-occupancy exemption failed, and the petition was dismissed with the occupant entitled to a lease in his name.

who_was_letting.quote: The subject building is a single-room occupancy (SRO) with four floors.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An occupant of an SRO room whom the owner alleged to be a squatter had continuously resided there since at least October 2008 and thus became a rent-stabilized "permanent tenant" entitled to a lease, regardless of any payment or formal agreement. The owner's squatter holdover petition was dismissed and the claimed owner-occupancy exemption rejected.

who_was_letting.quote: Based on the undisputed facts as established at trial, respondent is entitled to the protections of rent stabilization as the permanent tenant for the subject premises.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An occupant of an SRO building who continuously resided in a unit for more than six months with the owner's knowledge and acquiescence became a permanent tenant under the Rent Stabilization Code. The owner's squatter holdover proceeding was dismissed.

who_was_letting.quote: On June 15, 2009, petitioner entered into a written agreement to lease the property to seven Binghamton University students, for a term of approximately two years commencing on August 15, 2009 and ending on August 30, 2011.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The zoning board rationally found that seven university students leasing a single-family home in a single-unit district were not a "functional and factual family equivalent," so their occupancy violated the zoning ordinance. The board's determination was upheld, though the City could not use RPAPL 715 to compel eviction.

who_was_letting.quote: On June 15, 2009, petitioner entered into a written agreement to lease the property to seven Binghamton University students, for a term of approximately two years commencing on August 15, 2009 and ending on August 30, 2011.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court upheld the zoning board's determination that seven university students leasing a single-family home were not a functional and factual family equivalent and thus could not occupy the property under the ordinance. It nevertheless held that RPAPL 715 could not be used to compel their eviction because the tenants themselves had not used the premises for an illegal trade or business.

contested.name: 27 Jay Street, LLC v. City of New York

polarity.quote: Accordingly, it is adjudged that the petition is denied, and the proceeding is dismissed.
polarity.holding_summary: The court upheld the Loft Board's refusal to declare a loft apartment abandoned after the tenant departed in the ordinary course at the end of a month-to-month tenancy. Ordinary turnover, unlike abandonment, did not remove the unit from Loft Law coverage.

contested.name: Cooper v. Back on Track Group, Inc.

polarity.quote: The court finds BOT’s argument that licensees housed at BOT are exempt from statutory protections and may be subject to extrajudicial eviction unpersuasive and not grounded in fact or law.
polarity.holding_summary: An occupant of a bunk bed in a three-quarter house, for whom the city paid $215 per month, had resided there more than thirty days and could not be removed by self-help. The operator's 'waiver of participant rights' was an unconscionable contract of adhesion and unenforceable against the statutory protections of RPAPL 711 and the unlawful eviction provisions, and possession was restored.

polarity.quote: The court finds BOT’s argument that licensees housed at BOT are exempt from statutory protections and may be subject to extrajudicial eviction unpersuasive and not grounded in fact or law.
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that a three-quarter-house resident could not be excluded without legal process after more than 30 days of paid occupancy. The operator's license agreement and purported waiver of tenant rights were unenforceable as an unconscionable contract of adhesion.

polarity.quote: A tenant shall include an occupant of one or more rooms in a rooming house or a resident, not including a transient occupant, of one or more rooms in a hotel who has been in possession for thirty consecutive days or longer; he shall not be removed from possession except in a special proceeding.
polarity.holding_summary: A three-quarter house operator's attempt to categorize a paying resident as a mere 'participant' rather than a tenant, and to use self-help eviction, was rejected; the occupant, having resided over 30 days and paid rent via DSS, was entitled to statutory protections against unlawful eviction under RPAPL and the Administrative Code. The purported waiver of tenant rights was held unenforceable as unconscionable.

polarity.quote: that the plaintiff could not refuse to rent the rooms to other lodgers, leaving them idle, and then recover against the defendant, as for use and occupation
polarity.holding_summary: A householder who let rooms and furnished board to a family at $150 a week could sue for breach of the board-and-lodging contract, but her recovery was limited to actual damages, since she was bound to relet the rooms and could not leave them idle. The judgment was reduced (or a new trial ordered) because the full weekly price had been allowed for the vacancy period.

polarity.quote: a landlord who had let rooms, was not entitled as matter of course to recover from the tenant who had violated his contract, and abandoned the rooms, the whole price stipulated to be paid for the use of the rooms, to the end of the period specified in the contract, but only for such damages as had directly and necessarily resulted from the breach of the contract
polarity.holding_summary: The court addressed damages after a family breached a contract for rooms, board, and lodging. It held that the room provider could recover only damages directly resulting from the breach and could not leave rooms idle and recover the full contract price.

who_was_letting.quote: This action was brought to recover for damages resulting to plaintiff from an alleged breach, by defendant's testator, of a contract for board and lodging. Tbe evidence tended to show that plaintiff rented to defendant's testator certain rooms, and agreed to board bis family from September 1,1866, to May 1, 1867, for $150 a week.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A woman who rented rooms and agreed to board a family for an eight-month term at $150 a week sued for damages when the boarder breached and abandoned the rooms. The court enforced the board-and-lodging contract, affirming recovery of the rent differential after the rooms were relet, but held the landlord could not recover the full contract price for the vacant period and had a duty to mitigate. The letting arrangement was treated as an ordinary enforceable contract.

who_was_letting.quote: he engaged board and lodging for himself and family from tbe 1st September, 1866, to tbe 1st May, 1867
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A householder who let rooms and furnished board to a family at $150 a week could sue for breach of the board-and-lodging contract, but her recovery was limited to actual damages, since she was bound to relet the rooms and could not leave them idle. The judgment was reduced (or a new trial ordered) because the full weekly price had been allowed for the vacancy period.

contested.name: People ex rel. Board of Foreign Missions of the Methodist Episcopal Church v. Board of Assessors
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

who_was_letting.quote: Before it was acquired by the missionary society it had been a well-known boarding house.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A missionary board's Park Hill property, including a lodge with a hundred guest rooms and a public dining room, was let to guests for pay without distinction as to religious connection. The court held the property was used mainly as a hotel and business rather than exclusively for religious purposes, so the tax exemption was denied.

who_was_letting.quote: During the year 1920 guests were entertained there who were in nowise connected with the activities of the missionary society at all — in fact they appear to have been permanent • guests, paying their way just as they would have done at any other hotel.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that the missionary board's property was not tax-exempt because Wallace Lodge was operated substantially as a hotel serving paying members of the public. The operation was business use rather than an exclusively religious use, notwithstanding a preference for missionaries and religious workers.

contested.name: Maxwell v. Gerard
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, General Term

who_was_letting.quote: An innkeeper’s liability for the baggage of his guest is not termi- " nated tlie instant the guest pays his bill and leaves the hotel, but continues for such a reasonable time thereafter.as may be necessary for him to secure its removal
who_was_letting.holding_summary: An innkeeper's liability for a guest's baggage continues for a reasonable time after the guest pays and leaves, and until baggage the innkeeper undertook to forward is delivered. Judgment for the departed guest whose trunk was lost was affirmed.

who_was_letting.quote: An innkeeper’s liability for the baggage of his guest is not termi- " nated tlie instant the guest pays his bill and leaves the hotel, but continues for such a reasonable time thereafter.as may be necessary for him to secure its removal;
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that an innkeeper's liability for a guest's baggage continues for a reasonable time after the guest leaves or, where the innkeeper undertakes removal, until delivery is completed. The judgment for the guest was affirmed.

who_was_letting.quote: On the night of the 9th of that month the plaintiff went to said hotel or inn and became a guest thereof.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A hotel guest who deposited a satchel containing gold coin held by him as gratuitous bailee could recover from the innkeeper for its loss; the innkeeper's liability extends to all personal property of the guest brought to the inn and is not limited by kind or value absent statutory notice.

who_was_letting.quote: On the night of the 9th of that month the plaintiff went to said hotel or inn and became a guest thereof.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held an innkeeper liable to a hotel guest for gold stolen after the guest deposited a satchel with the hotel clerk. The innkeeper could not avoid liability based on the guest's use of a satchel or lack of specific disclosure of the gold's amount.

A gratuitous bailee who was a hotel guest could sue the innkeeper for the loss of coin belonging to a third party which he had deposited with the hotel, applying ordinary innkeeper-liability principles.

who_was_letting.quote: Inn-keepers are responsible, as .depositaries, for effects brought to their house by travelers who lodge therein
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Hotel keepers are liable as depositaries for the effects of travelers who lodge with them, including money stolen from a guest's trunk, absent proof of force majeure. The court noted they could have limited liability by posting the statutory notice.

who_was_letting.quote: Plaintiff, while on a journey to Washington City, stopped, in the latter part of the month of October, 1862, at the City Hotel in the city of New Orleans, where he lodged and deposited his trunk, containing seven hundred and eighteen dollars (five hundred and sixty-eight dollars of which amount belonged to him), some wearing apparel, official documents, etc.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court affirmed a judgment against hotel keepers for money stolen from a traveler's trunk while he lodged at their hotel. Innkeepers were liable as depositaries unless the statutory or Civil Code exceptions applied.

contested.name: Tower Insurance v. Corlette
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

who_was_letting.quote: The underlying personal injury action arose out of an incident in which the defendant Rosamone Beresford slipped and fell at a single-family residence owned by the defendant Jasmattie Corlette.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court affirmed a judgment requiring a homeowner's insurer to defend and indemnify the homeowner in a personal injury action, holding that the policy exclusion for injuries arising from rental of a single-family unit 'to lodge more than two roomers or boarders' did not apply on the facts. The court noted the term 'roomer' was undefined and that ambiguities are construed against the insurer.

who_was_letting.quote: a single family unit is intended for use by the occupying family to lodge more than two roomers or boarders
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A homeowner's policy excluded coverage where a single-family unit was intended to lodge more than two roomers or boarders, but the term 'roomer' was undefined. Construing the ambiguity against the insurer, the court held the exclusion inapplicable and the insurer obliged to defend and indemnify the homeowner.

contested.name: Stewart v. Briggs
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

polarity.quote: if, while so holding, he should let them to another, such tenant would be bound to pay him rent until evicted by the-city, and would be estopped from, denying his landlord’s title
polarity.holding_summary: An owner in possession of a farm whose fee had vested in the city by condemnation leased the house for one year for residential purposes. The court held she could lease and collect rent until the city actually took possession, and the tenant could not dispute her title or attorn to strangers.

polarity.quote: Until the city did take-possession, however, and so terminate his agreement with the plaintiff, he was bound to pay to her the rent stipulated by his contract.
polarity.holding_summary: The court held that the plaintiff, who remained in possession after the city's condemnation title vested, had a right to lease the house and collect rent until the city actually took possession. The tenant could not deny her title or refuse the agreed rent while his occupancy remained undisturbed.

contested.name: Atkinson v. Wilt
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

who_was_letting.quote: For seven weeks during the summer of 2010, petitioners rented the property on a weekly basis to various parties.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Owners of a six-bedroom second home who rented it by the week to vacationers for seven weeks in a summer were not operating a 'tourist accommodation' under the town ordinance, and their use remained that of a single-family residence. Zoning regulations being in derogation of the common law, ambiguity was resolved in favor of the owners and the zoning board's determination was annulled.

who_was_letting.quote: For seven weeks during the summer of 2010, petitioners rented the property on a weekly basis to various parties.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court upheld annulment of a zoning-board determination that owners' occasional weekly vacation rentals made their six-bedroom residence a prohibited tourist accommodation. The ordinance did not expressly prohibit renting the residence to vacationers, and ambiguities had to be resolved for the owners.

who_was_letting.quote: For seven weeks during the summer of 2010, petitioners rented the property on a weekly basis to various parties.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court affirmed annulment of a zoning board determination that owners' weekly vacation rentals of their six-bedroom single-family residence constituted a 'tourist accommodation,' holding the determination irrational. The court found nothing in the ordinance expressly prohibited renting the residence to vacationers, and that the rentals did not remove the property from the definition of a single-family residence, which includes a seasonal cottage.

who_was_letting.quote: A “tourist accommodation,” in turn, includes “any hotel, motel, resort, tourist cabin or similar transient facility used to house the general public, including an accessory restaurant” (Land Use Ordinance of Town of Arietta § 2.020).
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The Appellate Division affirmed the annulment of a ZBA determination classifying short-term weekly vacation rentals of a lakefront home as an impermissible tourist accommodation, holding that zoning regulations in derogation of common law must be strictly construed in favor of the property owner where rentals to vacationers are not expressly prohibited.

contested.name: City of New York v. 330 Continental
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division

polarity.quote: We conclude that the City has not demonstrated an entitlement to a preliminary injunction stopping this activity.
polarity.holding_summary: The court vacated a preliminary injunction against SRO apartment hotels renting some rooms to tourists for less than 30 days. The City had not shown that short-term rooms constituted a majority of units or that a minority transient use violated the class-A and zoning provisions.
