polarity.quote: the use of a significant portion of a class A apartment hotel for transient occupancy (however defined) is permissible so long as it remains true that the building is “occupied, as a rule, for permanent residence purposes” (Multiple Dwelling Law § 4 [8] [a]) and that the building is “used primarily for permanent occupancy” (ZR § 12-10).
polarity.holding_summary: The court denied the City's preliminary injunction seeking to stop SRO apartment hotel owners from renting units for periods of less than 30 days, holding that the zoning resolution and Multiple Dwelling Law permit a secondary transient use so long as the buildings are used 'primarily' or 'as a rule' for permanent occupancy. The court found the statutory terms 'transient' and 'permanent' vague and construed the ambiguity in favor of the property owners.

polarity.quote: it follows that no violation either of the ZR or of the certificate of occupancy would result from the use of a minority of the units in one of the buildings for nonpermanent or transient occupancy
polarity.holding_summary: The City's preliminary injunction against renting SRO apartment-hotel units for stays under thirty days was vacated: because the zoning resolution and Multiple Dwelling Law require only that such buildings be used 'primarily' or 'as a rule' for permanent occupancy, letting a minority of units to tourists violates neither, and the City failed to quantify the transient use. The City's underlying causes of action were nonetheless allowed to proceed.

who_was_letting.quote: Where the proof shows that a house has been leased for one month at a fixed price, and one-half of the amount paid in advanoe, and the lessor leases the house to another party, and puts him in possession before the end of the month, the Court will award such damages to the first lessee as the proof shows that he has sustained by the violation of the lease by the lessor.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A house let for one month at a fixed price with half the rent paid in advance created a complete one-month lease; the lessor who re-let the house and put another in possession before the month expired was liable in damages to the first lessee.

who_was_letting.quote: Where the proof shows that a house has been leased for one month at a fixed price, and one-half of the amount paid in advanoe, and the lessor leases the house to another party, and puts him in possession before the end of the month, the Court will award such damages to the first lessee as the proof shows that he has sustained by the violation of the lease by the lessor.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A lessor who rents a house for one month with advance rent paid and subsequently re-leases the premises to another party before the month expires is liable to the first lessee for damages caused by the breach of lease.

who_was_letting.quote: Where the proof shows that a house has been leased for one month at a fixed price, and one-half of the amount paid in advanoe, and the lessor leases the house to another party, and puts him in possession before the end of the month, the Court will award such damages to the first lessee as the proof shows that he has sustained by the violation of the lease by the lessor.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court affirmed damages for a lessee after the lessor rented the house to another person before the agreed one-month lease ended. The first lessee had a contractual right to the house for the full month.

who_was_letting.quote: the lease was complete for one month, and not for a half month only
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A house was leased for one month at $20 with half a month's rent paid in advance; before the month expired the lessor leased the house to another party and put him in possession. The court affirmed damages for the first lessee for the lessor's violation of the lease. The one-month letting was treated as a complete, enforceable lease, but the judgment runs against the owner for breaching it.

contested.name: Friedenstein v. Canning
contested.court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term

polarity.quote: The mere fact that an immoral woman lives in a house, or visits one, is not sufficient to show that the tenant keeps a bawdy house.
polarity.holding_summary: A lessee kept a boarding house for theatrical people under a lease permitting that use; the landlord sought to dispossess her on the ground the house was disorderly. The court held the police testimony failed to show any immoral use and that the mere presence or visits of immoral women does not make the house a bawdy house, so the dispossess order was reversed.

polarity.quote: The defendant positively denied that she kept a disorderly house, and said that she kept a boarding house for theatrical people; that two of the women there were visitors of some of the inmates, and that the other women were boarders;
polarity.holding_summary: The court reversed a dispossession order because the evidence did not show that the tenant was operating a disorderly house rather than the permitted boarding house. The mere residence or visit of an immoral woman did not establish a prohibited bawdy house.

A rooming-house operator's libel petition failed because the allegedly defamatory article referring to 'whorehouses around Union Station placarded as Rooming Houses' did not identify his particular house, and his innuendo was a mere conclusion not supported by the facts alleged. Demurrer properly sustained.

who_was_letting.quote: One may occupy property and pay for such occupancy without being a tenant of anyone.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A sublessee of a garage apartment and his family were, as to the owner's driveway, mere licensees by permission, not tenants of the new owner, since landlord-tenant relation arises only from contract. The purchaser owed them only the duty to avoid wilful, wanton, or active negligence, and was not liable for the child's injury.

who_was_letting.quote: Our appreciation of the facts of this case has led us to the conclusion that so far as concerns the question of the use of the driveway plaintiff and the members of his family were licensees by permission.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that the plaintiff and his family were not the new owner's tenants or subtenants, but were licensees by permission in their use of the driveway. Because the child was a licensee and there was no willful, wanton, or active negligence, the owner was not liable for her injuries.

polarity.quote: As we have said, we find no defect here and no fault in original construction, and therefore, the owner is not liable since the accident resulted either from fault of the tenant in unfastening the door and in permitting the subtenant to use it, or from negligence on the part of the subtenant, himself.
polarity.holding_summary: The court affirmed dismissal of a sublessee's injury claim because the unfloored attic area was not part of the dwelling space intended for use and the owner was not at fault. It stated that an owner may lease only part of a building and reserve other portions for other purposes or from dwelling use.

polarity.quote: We entertain no doubt that* an owner of a building may lease only a portion of his building, that he may set aside other portions for other purposes, or that he may set aside any portion as not contemplated for use for dwelling purposes, and we think that he has that right and may exercise it
polarity.holding_summary: A laborer who agreed to lease a room from the owner's tenant was injured in an unfloored attic space and sued the owner; the court affirmed dismissal, finding no defect or fault by the owner. The court affirmed that an owner may lease portions of his building and set aside other portions not intended for dwelling use, and is not liable to those who use such reserved portions.

who_was_letting.quote: the appellant, J. W. Webster, operator of a tourist camp, sued the appellee, W. A. Moore, for a debt of $42, for past due rent and for foreclosure of an alleged lien upon certain household goods of the alleged value of $75
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A tourist camp operator sued an occupant for past-due rent and to foreclose a lien on the occupant's household goods; the county court's dismissal for want of an appeal bond and missing papers was reversed and the cause remanded.

who_was_letting.quote: In that court the appellant, J. W. Webster, operator of a tourist camp, sued the appellee, W. A. Moore, for a debt of $42, for past due rent and for foreclosure of an alleged lien upon certain household goods of the alleged value of $75.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that the tourist-camp operator's suit for past-due rent was improperly dismissed for lack of cost or appeal bonds and for a missing sequestration writ. It reversed and remanded the case so the operator could pursue the rent claim and alleged lien.

polarity.holding_summary: A conviction for possession of wine for sale in a dry area was reversed because the trial court failed to charge on circumstantial evidence. The facts included a son renting a room in the family house to a couple, but the court expressed no view on the legality or character of that letting.

polarity.quote: about two months prior to the search, he had rented the room where the wine was found to a man and his wife, whose names he gave as Mr. and Mrs. Roy Jones
polarity.holding_summary: Conviction for possessing wine for sale in a dry area was reversed for failure to charge on circumstantial evidence, where the defendant's son had rented out the room in the house in which the wine was found and the defendant lived elsewhere at the tourist camp she operated.

contested.name: Fort Worth & D. C. Ry. Co. v. Mills

polarity.holding_summary: A railroad employee's family occupied outfit cars furnished by the employer in lieu of a section house; the court held the relationship was that of employer and employee, not landlord and tenant, since occupancy was tied to the employment contract and no rent was paid. Judgment for injuries from a defective step was reversed and rendered for the railway.

who_was_letting.holding_summary: A railroad employee's family occupied outfit cars furnished by the employer in lieu of a section house; the court held the relationship was that of employer and employee, not landlord and tenant, since occupancy was tied to the employment contract and no rent was paid. Judgment for injuries from a defective step was reversed and rendered for the railway.

polarity.quote: The premises were not demised to appellee for any term nor did he have any rights therein that were not connected with and indeed a part of the contract of employment.
polarity.holding_summary: A railroad employee occupied railroad-furnished outfit cars as living quarters incident to his employment as section foreman; his wife was injured on steps at a nearby platform. The court held the occupancy was not a true landlord-tenant relationship but incident to employment, and in any event the railroad owed no duty to repair absent agreement, reversing a plaintiff's judgment.

contested.name: Shvekh v. Zoning Hearing Board of Stroud Township

who_was_letting.quote: In the instant case, Shvekh does not use the Property as her primary residence and neither does her son-in-law.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Renting an entire single-family home to vacationers for short stays is not a 'tourist home,' which requires bedroom-by-bedroom rental; the ordinance did not prohibit such vacation rentals and the enforcement notice was reversed.

who_was_letting.quote: Mrs. Conques testified that she and her mother, Shvekh, reside at 228 Glenoak Drive, East Stroudsburg, and her husband lives in New Jersey, In light of these developments, the family decided to rent out the Property from time to time.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: The court held that renting the entire house to vacation groups did not fit the ordinance's definition of a tourist home, which required room-by-room rental. It reversed the enforcement notice because the ordinance did not prohibit the vacation-rental use.

who_was_letting.quote: In December 2015, the Garretts purchased the lake house located at 405 Peninsula Court in the Scenic View Estates in Granbury, Texas ("the Property").
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Owners of a lake house listed it on VRBO for short-term vacation rentals; neighbors sought to enjoin the practice under 'single family residence purposes' and anti-commercial deed restrictions. The court held the restrictions ambiguous as to duration and commercial character, resolved all doubts in favor of the owners' free and unrestricted use, and dissolved the temporary injunction against short-term rentals. Short-term rental for eating, sleeping, and other residential purposes is residential, not commercial, no matter how short the duration.

who_was_letting.quote: Because the restrictive covenants at issue are ambiguous and because we are required to resolve any ambiguity against Appellees Georgia Kaye Sympson and Clifford A. Hall Sr. and in favor of the Garretts’ free and unrestricted use of their property, we will reverse the trial court’s order granting the temporary injunction and we will order the temporary injunction dissolved.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Deed restrictions limiting lots to 'single family residence purposes' and prohibiting commercial use are ambiguous as applied to short-term vacation rentals, so they must be construed in favor of the owners' free and unrestricted use. The temporary injunction barring the owners' VRBO rentals was dissolved; short-term rental for eating and sleeping is residential, not commercial, use.

contested.name: Schack v. Prop. Owners Ass'n of Sunset Bay
contested.court: Court of Appeals of Texas, Corpus Christi-Edinburg

who_was_letting.quote: According to the testimony of Raub and his wife Rosa, their intention was to rent the Property to groups of vacationers, and they would maintain their permanent residence in nearby Portland, Texas.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: A property owner rented his vacation house to groups for stays of three to seven days; neighbors sued to stop the practice under covenants restricting lots to single-family dwelling use, household-unit occupancy, and no 'commercial enterprise.' Applying Tarr, the court held the dwelling restriction was structural only, the occupancy restriction did not prohibit short-term rentals, and the jury's finding of no commercial enterprise was factually sufficient; judgment for the owner was affirmed. The court expressly invoked the rule that the right to lease property for profit is an incident of ...

who_was_letting.quote: "The ownership of land, when the estate is a fee, carries with it the right to use the land in any manner not hurtful to others; and the right to lease it to others, and therefore derive profit, is an incident of such ownership."
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Subdivision covenants limiting lots to one single family dwelling unit, limiting occupancy to a family unit, and barring commercial enterprises did not prohibit an owner from renting his house to vacationers for three to seven days. The dwelling restriction was purely structural, the occupancy restriction did not impose a durational requirement, and the jury's finding of no commercial enterprise was supported because the commercial activity occurred off-site.

contested.name: Tarr v. Timberwood Park Owners Ass'n, Inc.

who_was_letting.quote: Two years later, after his employer transferred him to Houston, Tarr began advertising the home for rent on websites such as VRBO (short for Vacation Rentals by Owner).
who_was_letting.holding_summary: After moving to Houston for work, an owner rented his San Antonio home through VRBO under thirty-one short-term agreements of one to seven days each. The Supreme Court of Texas held that the restrictive covenants, which limited tracts to 'residential purposes' and a 'single family residence,' unambiguously imposed no minimum-duration or owner-occupancy requirement, and that short-term rentals for living purposes are residential, not commercial, use. Summary judgment for the association was reversed; courts may not inject restrictions into covenants under the guise of interpretation.

who_was_letting.quote: We hold that Tarr has not violated the Timberwood restrictive covenants by entering into short-term vacation rental agreements.
who_was_letting.holding_summary: Covenants restricting tracts to 'residential purposes' and requiring that any building be a 'single family residence' do not prohibit short-term vacation rentals; the single-family clause is a structural limitation and the residential-purpose clause is silent as to leasing or minimum occupancy duration. So long as occupants use the home for ordinary living purposes, however briefly, neither their use nor the owner's off-site rental activity violates the covenants.
